lessons.title: Trigonometry
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Apply sin, cos, tan to right triangles
lessons.reading_material: Trigonometry studies relationships between angles and sides in triangles. In a right-angled triangle: SOH CAH TOA. sin(θ) = Opposite/Hypotenuse. cos(θ) = Adjacent/Hypotenuse. tan(θ) = Opposite/Adjacent. Example: ladder 10m long against wall, angle 60° — height = 10 × sin(60°) = 10 × 0.866 = 8.66m. Used in surveying, navigation, engineering!
practical_activities: Clinometer building height measurement
Map bearing problems
Architecture angle calculations

exercises.q: In a right triangle, opp=8, hyp=10. Find the angle.

homework.task: Using a clinometer (make with protractor and string), measure the height of a tree or building.

revision.notes: SOH: sin=O/H. CAH: cos=A/H. TOA: tan=O/A. Use inverse (sin⁻¹) to find angle from ratio.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Functions and Graphs
lessons.subject: Math
learning_objectives: Sketch and interpret graphs of functions
lessons.reading_material: A FUNCTION maps each input to exactly one output. Written f(x) = expression. f(3) means evaluate when x=3. Key functions: LINEAR f(x)=mx+c (straight line), QUADRATIC f(x)=ax²+bx+c (parabola), EXPONENTIAL f(x)=aˣ (rapid growth/decay). Key features: x-intercepts (roots), y-intercept, turning points, gradient, domain and range.
practical_activities: Graph different functions using technology
Identify function types from equations
Real-world function modelling (population growth)

homework.task: Sketch graphs of: y=2x+1, y=x²−4, y=2ˣ. Label key features on each.

revision.notes: f(x): substitue x to find y. Linear=straight, Quadratic=parabola, Exponential=J-curve. Domain=inputs, range=outputs.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Statistics: Hypothesis Testing
lessons.subject: Math
lessons.reading_material: Statistical hypothesis testing helps us make decisions based on data. NULL HYPOTHESIS (H₀): assumes no effect. ALTERNATIVE HYPOTHESIS (H₁): what we're trying to prove. We collect data, calculate a test statistic, and compare to a critical value. If our result is unlikely under H₀ (p-value < 0.05), we reject H₀. Used in science, medicine, and social research.
practical_activities: Survey class and test hypothesis about preferences
Analyse experimental data for significance
Design a statistical investigation

exercises.q: If p-value = 0.02, with significance level 0.05, we?

exercises.answer: The null hypothesis — no effect or no difference

homework.task: Design a hypothesis test: 'Students who sleep 8+ hours score higher in tests.' Plan data collection method.

revision.notes: H₀=no effect. Reject H₀ if p<0.05. Chi-squared tests categorical data. Always consider sample size.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Shakespeare: Language and Context
lessons.subject: English
learning_objectives: Analyse Shakespeare's use of dramatic techniques
Write an analytical essay on a Shakespeare play
lessons.reading_material: William Shakespeare (1564–1616) wrote 37 plays and 154 sonnets. His work explores universal themes: love, power, jealousy, ambition, fate. KEY TECHNIQUES: soliloquy (character speaks alone to audience), aside (whispered to audience), dramatic irony (audience knows what characters don't), iambic pentameter (10-syllable rhythmic pattern: da-DUM da-DUM...). Context: Elizabethan world view — great chain of being, divine right of kings, role of women.
practical_activities: Annotate a key soliloquy
Perform a scene in groups
Write 'To be or not to be' analysis

exercises.q: A soliloquy is when a character?

exercises.answer: When the audience knows something the characters do not, creating tension or humour

homework.task: Write an analytical paragraph on Macbeth's ambition. Use PEEL, include a quotation, and comment on Elizabethan context.

revision.notes: Tragedy: protagonist's fatal flaw leads to downfall. Comedy: ends in marriage/reunion. Iambic pentameter: 10 syllables, da-DUM pattern.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Evolution and Natural Selection
lessons.subject: Science
lessons.reading_material: Charles Darwin proposed that species change over time through natural selection. Organisms with advantageous traits survive and reproduce more. Over generations, these traits become more common. Evidence: fossil record, comparative anatomy, DNA similarities.
practical_activities: Examine beak variation in Darwin's finch simulation
Research antibiotic resistance as evolution

homework.task: Research one example of evolution happening today (bacteria or animals)

revision.notes: Variation + Selection + Reproduction = Evolution over time.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Periodic Table and Chemical Bonding
lessons.subject: Science
learning_objectives: Explain organisation of the Periodic Table
lessons.reading_material: The Periodic Table organises elements by atomic number. Elements in the same group have similar properties. Metals are on the left; non-metals on the right. Ionic bonding: metal transfers electrons to non-metal (e.g., NaCl). Covalent bonding: atoms share electrons (e.g., H₂O).
practical_activities: Build ionic bond model with clay
Dot-and-cross diagrams for NaCl and H₂O

exercises.q: What type of bond forms in water (H₂O)?

homework.task: Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for NaCl and CO₂

revision.notes: Ionic = transfer electrons. Covalent = share electrons.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Energy Resources and Management
lessons.subject: Geography
learning_objectives: Evaluate the transition to renewable energy
lessons.reading_material: The world relies on fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) for ~80% of energy. These produce greenhouse gases and will run out. Renewable alternatives: solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, tidal. Energy mix varies by country (Saudi Arabia = oil; Iceland = geothermal). Energy security is critical for development.
practical_activities: Compare energy mixes of 5 countries using data
Evaluate a proposed wind farm — pros and cons

exercises.q: What percentage of global energy comes from fossil fuels approximately?

homework.task: Research the energy mix of your country and one renewable it could expand

revision.notes: Fossil fuels = limited + polluting. Renewables = clean + sustainable but have limitations too.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Geopolitics and Conflict
lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.reading_material: Geopolitics studies how geography affects international relations and power. Nations conflict over territory, water, oil, and strategic routes. The South China Sea has disputes over islands and resources. Water scarcity causes conflict in river basin nations. International organisations (UN) mediate disputes.
practical_activities: Map current territorial disputes
Debate: how should the UN handle a water conflict?

options: How geography affects politics and power
exercises.answer: How geography affects politics and power

homework.task: Research one ongoing territorial dispute and its background

revision.notes: Geography shapes power. Resources and territory cause conflict. Diplomacy aims to resolve.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Historiography: How We Know the Past
lessons.subject: World History
learning_objectives: Evaluate different types of historical sources
lessons.reading_material: Historiography is the study of how history is written and interpreted. Primary sources: direct evidence (diaries, letters, artefacts). Secondary sources: later interpretations (books, documentaries). Historians must evaluate: bias, provenance, context, purpose. Revisionist historians challenge established narratives. Postcolonial history re-centres non-European perspectives.
practical_activities: Analyse the same event from two different national perspectives
Identify bias in a historical text

homework.task: Find two accounts of the same historical event — identify any differences in perspective

revision.notes: Primary = direct evidence. Secondary = later interpretation. Always check bias and provenance.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.q: What does provenance mean in historical analysis?
options: The origin and context of a source
questions.answer: The origin and context of a source

lessons.title: Human Rights and Global Justice
lessons.subject: World History
learning_objectives: Trace the development of international human rights law
lessons.reading_material: Human rights are fundamental rights every person has by virtue of being human. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR, 1948) established 30 rights. International bodies (ICC, UNHCR) protect rights. Key issues: genocide, refugees, women's rights, freedom of expression. Rights abuses still occur despite international law.
practical_activities: Analyse one article of the UDHR in depth
Case study: Rwandan genocide and international response

homework.task: Choose one human right and research a country where it is currently threatened

revision.notes: UDHR 1948 = 30 universal rights. ICC enforces. Tension: sovereignty vs humanitarian intervention.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

criteria: Analyses one case of rights abuse

lessons.title: Islamic Civilisation and Contributions
lessons.subject: Islamic Studies
learning_objectives: Identify key contributions of Islamic civilisation
Explain the Golden Age of Islam
Appreciate the Islamic legacy in science, medicine, and philosophy
lessons.reading_material: Between the 8th and 13th centuries, the Islamic world led the world in science, medicine, mathematics, philosophy, and art. Scholars like Al-Khwarizmi (algebra), Ibn Sina (medicine), Al-Biruni (geography), and Al-Ghazali (philosophy) transformed human knowledge.
practical_activities: Research one Islamic scholar and present their contribution
Create a timeline of Islamic civilisation achievements
exercises: Name 3 Islamic scholars and their fields
Explain the importance of the House of Wisdom in Baghdad
lessons.homework: Research how one contribution of Islamic civilisation still impacts your life today.

revision.notes: The word 'algebra' comes from the Arabic 'al-jabr' — a direct legacy of Islamic scholarship.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: Which Islamic scholar is known as the father of algebra?
What was the House of Wisdom?
options: A great centre of learning in Baghdad
questions.correct: A great centre of learning in Baghdad

lessons.assessment: Write a research report on one aspect of Islamic civilisation and its lasting impact.

lessons.title: Object-Oriented Programming
lessons.subject: Coding
learning_objectives: Define a class with attributes and methods
lessons.reading_material: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) organises code around 'objects' — instances of 'classes'. A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance. Attributes store data; methods define behaviour.
practical_activities: Build a Student class with name, grade, and a display method
Create multiple student objects
exercises: Add a method that returns the student's grade as a letter
Create a BankAccount class with deposit and withdraw methods
lessons.homework: Build a library system: Book class with title, author, and a checkout() method.

revision.notes: Think of a class like a cookie cutter and an object like the cookie — same shape, different dough.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Post-Colonial Literature
lessons.subject: World Literature
learning_objectives: Analyse how authors reclaim cultural identity
Evaluate the political dimensions of world literature
lessons.reading_material: Post-colonial literature emerged after the end of European empires. Writers reclaimed language, culture, and history. Key authors: Chinua Achebe (Nigeria) — 'Things Fall Apart' directly responds to Conrad's 'Heart of Darkness'. Salman Rushdie (India/UK) — magic realism in 'Midnight's Children'. Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie (Nigeria) — 'Purple Hibiscus', warns of 'the danger of a single story'. Derek Walcott (St Lucia) won the Nobel Prize for poetry that blends African, European, and Caribbean traditions. Post-colonial themes: identity, hybridity, language and power, resistance, and remembering.
practical_activities: Read Adichie's TED Talk 'The Danger of a Single Story' — class discussion on how we can broaden our reading
exercises: What is 'hybridity' in post-colonial literature?
How does Achebe challenge Conrad in 'Things Fall Apart'?
Why is language a form of power in colonial contexts?
lessons.homework: Research one post-colonial author from your region — read an excerpt and write a short analysis.

revision.notes: Post-colonial lit reclaims identity and history. Key ideas: hybridity, resistance, language as power.
revision.tip: 'The single story creates stereotypes' — Adichie. Always seek multiple perspectives.

quiz.question: 'Hybridity' in post-colonial theory refers to
options: A mix of coloniser and colonised cultural elements
quiz.correct: A mix of coloniser and colonised cultural elements

lessons.assessment: Write a 300-word essay: 'How does post-colonial literature challenge the legacy of colonialism?' — use TWO texts as evidence.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Kite
info_cards.fact: "The Kite" by Francisco Goya. An early tapestry-design painting by Goya showing young men flying a kite outdoors.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Two Tahitian Women
info_cards.fact: "Two Tahitian Women" by Paul Gauguin. A painting from Gauguin's time in Tahiti, known for its bold tropical colours.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?
info_cards.fact: "Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?" by Paul Gauguin. A large, philosophical painting exploring the stages of human life.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Yellow Christ
info_cards.fact: "The Yellow Christ" by Paul Gauguin. A Post-Impressionist painting showing a crucifix scene in a Brittany landscape.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Bedroom
info_cards.fact: "The Bedroom" by Vincent van Gogh. Another version of Van Gogh's painting of his simple bedroom in Arles.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Irises
info_cards.fact: "Irises" by Vincent van Gogh. A vivid painting of purple irises growing in a garden.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Almond Blossoms
info_cards.fact: "Almond Blossoms" by Vincent van Gogh. A painting of blooming almond branches against a blue sky, made to celebrate a birth in his family.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: The Potato Eaters
info_cards.fact: "The Potato Eaters" by Vincent van Gogh. An early Van Gogh painting showing a poor farming family sharing a meal.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Sunflowers in a Vase
info_cards.fact: "Sunflowers in a Vase" by Vincent van Gogh. Another of Van Gogh's sunflower still-life paintings made in Arles.

info_cards.title: Famous Painting: Boulevard Montmartre
info_cards.fact: "Boulevard Montmartre" by Camille Pissarro. An Impressionist street scene of a busy Paris boulevard.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Abraham Lincoln: The Man (Standing Lincoln)
info_cards.fact: "Abraham Lincoln: The Man (Standing Lincoln)" by Augustus Saint-Gaudens. A bronze statue of President Lincoln standing in Chicago's Lincoln Park.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Puck Statue
info_cards.fact: "The Puck Statue" by Frederick William MacMonnies. A bronze statue of the mischievous character Puck atop a New York building.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Dreaming Girl
info_cards.fact: "The Dreaming Girl" by Edward Berge. A bronze fountain sculpture of a sleeping figure, in Baltimore's Wyman Park.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Storyteller
info_cards.fact: "The Storyteller" by Glenna Goodacre. A bronze public sculpture celebrating the tradition of oral storytelling.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Vietnam Women's Memorial
info_cards.fact: "Vietnam Women's Memorial" by Glenna Goodacre. A bronze sculpture in Washington, D.C., honouring women who served during the Vietnam War.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Ireland's Famine Memorial
info_cards.fact: "Ireland's Famine Memorial" by Rowan Gillespie. A group of bronze statues in Dublin honouring those who endured the Great Famine.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: The Matchstick Men
info_cards.fact: "The Matchstick Men" by Sean Hanley (after L. S. Lowry). Public sculptures inspired by a beloved English painter's depiction of working-class life.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Bronze Lions of Trafalgar Square
info_cards.fact: "Bronze Lions of Trafalgar Square" by Edwin Landseer. Four large bronze lion statues guarding the base of Nelson's Column in London.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Eros Statue (Piccadilly Circus)
info_cards.fact: "Eros Statue (Piccadilly Circus)" by Alfred Gilbert. A famous bronze and aluminium fountain statue in central London.

info_cards.title: Famous Sculpture: Peter Pan Statue (Kensington Gardens)
info_cards.fact: "Peter Pan Statue (Kensington Gardens)" by George Frampton. A bronze statue of the storybook character, standing in a London park.

lessons.title: Design and Typography
lessons.subject: Art
lessons.reading_material: Graphic design communicates through images, layout, and typography. Principles include: hierarchy (most important = biggest), contrast, alignment, repetition, and proximity. Typography choices convey tone and personality.
practical_activities: Analyse the design of 3 posters or adverts
Design an event poster applying design principles
exercises: Identify hierarchy in a magazine spread
Choose and justify font choices for a brand
lessons.homework: Redesign an existing poster using at least 3 graphic design principles.

revision.notes: Less is more — clear hierarchy and whitespace are more powerful than clutter.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.correct: Making the most important element visually dominant

questions.question: What is whitespace?
options: Deliberate empty space used to improve clarity and balance
questions.correct: Deliberate empty space used to improve clarity and balance

lessons.title: Composition and Songwriting
lessons.subject: Music
learning_objectives: Layer rhythm and melody to create texture
lessons.reading_material: Composition is the art of organising music. Great compositions use repetition (to create familiarity), contrast (to create interest), and variation (to develop material). An 8-bar structure (A-A-B-A) is a common form.
practical_activities: Compose an 8-bar melody using a pentatonic scale
Add a rhythmic accompaniment pattern
exercises: Identify repetition, contrast, and variation in a song
Write a motif and develop it into a 4-bar melody
lessons.homework: Compose a 16-bar piece in A-A-B-A form using at least 2 instruments or voice parts.

revision.notes: A strong motif (short musical idea) is the seed for a whole composition — develop it with repetition and variation.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

lessons.title: Disaster Preparedness
lessons.subject: Survival Skills
learning_objectives: Identify natural disasters relevant to your region
lessons.reading_material: Natural disasters include earthquakes, floods, hurricanes/cyclones, wildfires, and tsunamis. A 72-hour emergency kit should contain: 3 litres of water per person per day, non-perishable food, first aid kit, torch (flashlight) and batteries, mobile phone and charger, copies of important documents, cash, medication, and a whistle. Family emergency plan: meeting points (near home and away from home), out-of-town contact, evacuation route. Earthquake: Drop, Cover, Hold On. Flood: move to high ground immediately — never drive through floodwater.
practical_activities: Build and present a 72-hour emergency kit — justify every item included
exercises: What is in a 72-hour emergency kit?
Explain 'Drop, Cover, Hold On' for earthquakes
What should you do if a flood warning is issued?
lessons.homework: Create a family emergency plan with two meeting points and an out-of-area contact.

revision.notes: 72-hour kit: water, food, first aid, torch, documents, cash, medication. Earthquake: Drop, Cover, Hold On.
revision.tip: Check and update your kit every 6 months — water expires and batteries drain.

quiz.question: A 72-hour kit should include how much water per person per day?

lessons.assessment: Design and present a complete family emergency plan for a specific natural disaster scenario.
textbook_references: Red Cross Disaster Preparedness for Schools

lessons.title: Advanced Cooking Techniques
lessons.subject: Cooking
learning_objectives: Apply advanced techniques: sautéing, braising, tempering chocolate
Explain the science behind each technique
lessons.reading_material: Advanced cooking techniques elevate dishes. Sautéing: cook quickly in a little fat at high heat to retain colour and texture. Braising: slow-cook in liquid (stock/wine) to tenderise tough cuts. Poaching: gentle simmering in liquid for delicate proteins (eggs, fish). Tempering chocolate: carefully control temperature (melt to 50°C, cool to 27°C, reheat to 32°C) to produce glossy, snappy chocolate. Sensory analysis evaluates food by appearance, aroma, taste, texture, and aftertaste.
practical_activities: Prepare a braised dish — document each step with photos and write a sensory analysis
exercises: Explain the difference between sautéing and braising
At what temperature is chocolate tempered?
Design a sensory analysis scoring sheet for a given dish
lessons.homework: Try tempering chocolate at home (with supervision) and evaluate the results.

revision.notes: Sauté = hot + fast + little fat. Braise = slow + liquid. Temper chocolate at 27°C (cool stage).
revision.tip: Mise en place (everything in place before cooking) is the professional chef's first rule.

lessons.assessment: Cook and present one advanced technique dish — scored on technique, taste, and presentation.

lessons.title: Arabic Literature — Poetry and Prose
lessons.subject: Foreign Languages
learning_objectives: Identify literary devices in Arabic text
Write an original piece in Arabic
lessons.reading_material: Arabic literature is among the world's richest. Classical poetry used strict metres (بحور الشعر) and rhyme schemes. The Mu'allaqat are pre-Islamic odes considered masterpieces. Al-Mutanabbi (10th century) is considered one of the greatest Arabic poets. Modern Arabic literature includes Nobel laureate Naguib Mahfouz (نجيب محفوظ) whose novel 'Palace Walk' depicts Egyptian life. Literary devices in Arabic: تشبيه (simile), استعارة (metaphor), جناس (pun/wordplay).
practical_activities: Read an excerpt from a Mahfouz novel in Arabic and discuss its themes and literary devices
exercises: Name two classical and one modern Arabic literary figure
Identify تشبيه in a given poem
Write 4 lines of Arabic free verse on a theme of your choice
lessons.homework: Read a short poem by Al-Mutanabbi — find one simile and explain it.

revision.notes: Classical Arabic poetry: strict metre and rhyme. Modern: Mahfouz. Devices: تشبيه، استعارة.
revision.tip: Arabic literary vocabulary is different from everyday vocabulary — build a specialist word list.

quiz.question: Who is considered one of the greatest classical Arabic poets?
تشبيه in Arabic literary terms means

lessons.assessment: Write a 150-word analysis of one literary device in a given Arabic poem excerpt.
textbook_references: Arabic Literature — Selections from Abbasid and Modern Periods

info_cards.title: Famous Places
info_cards.fact: The Colosseum in Rome could hold an estimated 50,000-80,000 spectators for gladiatorial contests and public spectacles.

info_cards.title: Philosophical Quote
info_cards.fact: "The only true wisdom is in knowing you know nothing." — Socrates.

info_cards.title: Famous Quote
info_cards.fact: "Float like a butterfly, sting like a bee." — Muhammad Ali.

info_cards.title: Famous Person: Ada Lovelace
info_cards.fact: Ada Lovelace, a 19th-century English mathematician, is regarded as the first computer programmer for her work on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: The Diary of a Young Girl
info_cards.fact: Anne Frank's diary records her life in hiding during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands, offering a firsthand account of the Holocaust through a teenager's eyes.

info_cards.title: Book Summary: The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind
info_cards.fact: "The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind" by William Kamkwamba tells how a teenager in Malawi built a windmill from scrap parts to bring electricity to his family's home.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Marcus Aurelius
info_cards.fact: "You have power over your mind, not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength." — Roman emperor and Stoic philosopher whose personal writings, Meditations, remain widely read today.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Lao Tzu
info_cards.fact: "A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step." — Ancient Chinese philosopher traditionally credited as the founder of Taoism and author of the Tao Te Ching.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Ibn Khaldun
info_cards.fact: "History is a science... it has a great utility, an honorable purpose, since it makes us acquainted with the conditions of past nations." — Arab historian and scholar often regarded as a founder of sociology and historiography.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Maimonides
info_cards.fact: "Teach thy tongue to say 'I do not know,' and thou shalt progress." — Medieval Jewish philosopher and physician whose writings shaped Jewish law and philosophy.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Thomas Aquinas
info_cards.fact: "To one who has faith, no explanation is necessary. To one without faith, no explanation is possible." — Italian Dominican friar and philosopher whose writings blended Christian theology with Aristotelian philosophy.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Voltaire
info_cards.fact: "Common sense is not so common." — French Enlightenment writer and philosopher known for his advocacy of free speech and religious tolerance.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: John Locke
info_cards.fact: "The discipline of desire is the background of character." — English philosopher whose ideas about natural rights influenced modern democracy and the U.S. Constitution.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Mary Wollstonecraft
info_cards.fact: "I do not wish women to have power over men, but over themselves." — English writer and philosopher often considered a founder of feminist philosophy for her book A Vindication of the Rights of Woman.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Immanuel Kant
info_cards.fact: "Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law." — German philosopher whose work on ethics and reason deeply influenced modern philosophy.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Friedrich Nietzsche
info_cards.fact: "He who has a why to live for can bear almost any how." — German philosopher known for his ideas on morality, culture, and the concept of the 'will to power.'

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Soren Kierkegaard
info_cards.fact: "Life is not a problem to be solved, but a reality to be experienced." — Danish philosopher often considered the first existentialist philosopher.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Simone de Beauvoir
info_cards.fact: "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman." — French philosopher and writer whose book The Second Sex became a foundational text of feminist theory.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Bertrand Russell
info_cards.fact: "The whole problem with the world is that fools and fanatics are always so certain of themselves." — British philosopher and mathematician who won the Nobel Prize in Literature for his wide-ranging humanist writing.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Hannah Arendt
info_cards.fact: "The sad truth is that most evil is done by people who never make up their minds to be either good or evil." — German-American political theorist known for her writings on totalitarianism and political power.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Rumi
info_cards.fact: "Let yourself be silently drawn by the strange pull of what you really love." — 13th-century Persian poet and Sufi mystic whose poetry remains widely read and translated today.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Al-Farabi
info_cards.fact: "The First Cause is the cause of the existence of every other existent." — Medieval philosopher known as 'the Second Teacher' (after Aristotle) for his influence on Islamic philosophy.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Averroes (Ibn Rushd)
info_cards.fact: "Ignorance leads to fear, fear leads to hatred, and hatred leads to violence." — Andalusian philosopher and judge whose commentaries on Aristotle influenced both Islamic and European thought.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Zhuangzi
info_cards.fact: "Flow with whatever may happen, and let your mind be free." — Ancient Chinese philosopher whose writings, alongside Lao Tzu's, form a foundation of Taoist thought.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Mencius
info_cards.fact: "The great man is he who does not lose his child's heart." — Chinese philosopher and follower of Confucius whose writings shaped Confucian thought on human nature.

info_cards.title: Notable Person: Seneca
info_cards.fact: "Luck is what happens when preparation meets opportunity." — Roman Stoic philosopher and statesman whose letters and essays remain widely studied today.

lessons.title: Technology and the Digital World
lessons.subject: General Knowledge
learning_objectives: Evaluate the impact of AI and automation
lessons.reading_material: We live in a digital age where technology shapes every aspect of life. Artificial Intelligence (AI) enables machines to learn and make decisions. Automation is replacing routine jobs but creating new ones. Social media connects billions but raises concerns about misinformation and mental health. Cybersecurity protects data from hackers. The Fourth Industrial Revolution (Industry 4.0) combines physical, digital, and biological systems. Digital literacy — the ability to use, evaluate, and create digital content — is a fundamental 21st-century skill.
practical_activities: Debate: Is AI more of a benefit or a threat to society?
exercises: Define AI and give two examples of it in daily life
What are two benefits and two risks of social media?
Explain what a strong password does and why it matters
lessons.homework: Research a job that AI is changing — explain what parts are automated and what still needs humans.

revision.notes: AI = machines that learn. Cybersecurity = protecting digital data. Digital literacy is essential in the 21st century.
revision.tip: Stay curious about new technologies but always question their impact on society.

lessons.assessment: Write a 300-word analysis of how ONE technology trend is changing education.

lessons.title: Globalisation
lessons.subject: Social Studies
learning_objectives: Analyse benefits and drawbacks of globalisation
Evaluate its impact on culture and employment
lessons.reading_material: Globalisation is the process by which the world's economies, cultures, and populations have become increasingly interconnected through trade, technology, and migration. Benefits: economic growth, cultural exchange, access to goods and ideas. Drawbacks: cultural homogenisation (local cultures threatened), exploitation of cheap labour in developing countries, environmental damage from increased transport, and economic inequality. Multinational corporations (MNCs) operate across borders, bringing investment but also sometimes avoiding taxes and suppressing local competition.
practical_activities: Analyse a global brand (e.g. Nike) — where are its products made, sold, and marketed?
exercises: Define globalisation in your own words
Give two benefits and two drawbacks of globalisation
What is a multinational corporation?
lessons.homework: Track one product (e.g. a t-shirt) from raw material to your wardrobe — how many countries are involved?

revision.notes: Globalisation = interconnected world economy and culture. Benefits AND drawbacks must both be considered.
revision.tip: Think about what you're wearing right now — it likely crossed several borders to reach you.

quiz.question: Globalisation primarily refers to
options: Increasing global interconnection through trade and technology
quiz.correct: Increasing global interconnection through trade and technology

lessons.assessment: Write a 300-word essay: 'Is globalisation more beneficial or harmful?' — argue ONE side with evidence.

lessons.title: Climate Science and Policy
lessons.subject: Environmental Science
learning_objectives: Explain the science behind climate change
lessons.reading_material: Scientific consensus: human activities (burning fossil fuels) increase CO₂, enhancing the greenhouse effect, causing global warming. IPCC reports synthesise research. Paris Agreement (2015): nations commit to limit warming to 1.5–2°C above pre-industrial levels. Mitigation: reducing emissions. Adaptation: adjusting to changes. Carbon pricing, renewable energy, and international cooperation are key policies.
practical_activities: Analyse IPCC report data
Debate: is the Paris Agreement sufficient?

exercises.q: What does the Paris Agreement aim to limit?
options: Global warming to 1.5–2°C above pre-industrial levels
exercises.answer: Global warming to 1.5–2°C above pre-industrial levels

homework.task: Research your country's climate commitments under the Paris Agreement

revision.notes: IPCC = scientific body. Paris Agreement = global climate treaty. Mitigation + Adaptation both needed.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.q: What is the difference between mitigation and adaptation?
options: Mitigation reduces emissions; adaptation adjusts to change
questions.answer: Mitigation reduces emissions; adaptation adjusts to change

lessons.title: Exercise Physiology Basics
lessons.subject: Physical Education & Self-Defense
learning_objectives: Explain aerobic and anaerobic energy systems
Describe the effect of training on the body
lessons.reading_material: Aerobic exercise uses oxygen to produce energy — sustainable for longer duration (jogging, swimming). Anaerobic exercise does not use oxygen — produces energy quickly but unsustainably (sprinting). Training causes adaptations: lower resting heart rate, greater lung capacity, stronger muscles.
practical_activities: Compare heart rate during aerobic vs anaerobic exercise
Calculate training zones from maximum heart rate
exercises: Explain why your breathing rate increases during exercise
Calculate your maximum heart rate (220 - age) and training zones
lessons.homework: Design a 6-week training programme targeting cardiovascular improvement.

revision.notes: Aerobic means 'with oxygen'. Aerobic exercise: you can still hold a conversation. Anaerobic: you cannot.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: What energy system is used during a 100m sprint?
What is a common adaptation to regular aerobic training?

lessons.assessment: Create a heart rate response graph and annotate the aerobic and anaerobic zones.

lessons.title: Markets and Price Mechanism
lessons.subject: Economics
learning_objectives: Predict price changes from market shifts
lessons.reading_material: In a free market, price is determined by supply and demand. The demand curve slopes downward (as price rises, quantity demanded falls). The supply curve slopes upward (as price rises, more is supplied). Equilibrium: where supply equals demand — the market-clearing price. Shifts in demand (new technology, income changes) or supply (input costs, technology) move the equilibrium. Price acts as a signal and incentive in markets.
practical_activities: Draw supply and demand diagrams for 3 given scenarios and predict equilibrium changes
exercises: Draw a supply and demand diagram for apples — label axes, curves, and equilibrium
If income rises, how does demand for luxury goods shift? Show on a diagram
What happens to equilibrium price if supply falls (ceteris paribus)?
lessons.homework: Track the price of one commodity (e.g. petrol, eggs) for two weeks — explain changes using supply/demand.

revision.notes: Supply ↑ → price ↓. Demand ↑ → price ↑. Equilibrium = market clears. Draw diagrams to show shifts.
revision.tip: Label diagrams clearly — examiners can't read minds, only labels.

quiz.question: On a demand curve, as price rises, quantity demanded

lessons.assessment: Analyse a given market scenario using supply/demand diagrams — predict and explain equilibrium change.

lessons.title: Banking and Saving
lessons.subject: Finance
lessons.reading_material: Banks accept deposits and lend money, charging borrowers more interest than they pay savers. A savings account earns interest — money the bank pays you for storing your money. Simple interest: I = P × R × T (Principal × Rate × Time). Compound interest earns interest on top of interest, growing wealth faster. Example: £1,000 at 5% compound interest for 10 years grows to £1,629. The earlier you start saving, the more compound interest works in your favour.
practical_activities: Calculate compound interest using a spreadsheet — chart growth over 20 years
exercises: Calculate simple interest on £500 at 4% for 3 years
Explain compound interest with a numerical example
Why should you start saving early?
lessons.homework: Research the best savings account interest rate at a local bank and calculate what £500 would grow to in 5 years.

revision.notes: Simple interest = P×R×T. Compound interest = grows on accumulated interest. Start saving early!
revision.tip: Use the rule of 72: divide 72 by interest rate to find years to double money.

quiz.question: Compound interest differs from simple interest because
options: Interest is earned on previously earned interest
quiz.correct: Interest is earned on previously earned interest

quiz.question: The Rule of 72 estimates
options: Years to double money at a given interest rate
quiz.correct: Years to double money at a given interest rate

lessons.assessment: Calculate compound interest on £2,000 at 6% for 5 years — show all working.

lessons.title: CPR and AED
lessons.subject: First Aid
learning_objectives: Respond to a cardiac arrest scenario
lessons.reading_material: Cardiac arrest happens when the heart stops beating. CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation) keeps blood circulating until help arrives. Hands-only CPR: 30 chest compressions (hard and fast, at least 5–6 cm deep, 100–120 per minute) at the centre of the chest, then 2 rescue breaths (if trained). AED (Automated External Defibrillator) delivers an electric shock to restart the heart. AEDs give audio instructions and are safe for untrained users. Chain of survival: early recognition → call for help → CPR → AED → advanced care.
practical_activities: Practise CPR on a mannequin at the correct depth and rate — use a metronome at 110 bpm
exercises: Describe the correct hand position for CPR
How deep should chest compressions be?
What is the compression-to-breath ratio for CPR?
lessons.homework: Research the location of the nearest AED to your school and describe the chain of survival steps.

revision.notes: CPR: 30 compressions + 2 breaths. Depth 5-6cm. Rate 100-120/min. AED follows audio instructions.
revision.tip: Sing 'Stayin' Alive' (104 bpm) to keep the correct compression rhythm.

lessons.assessment: Demonstrate hands-only CPR on a mannequin for 2 minutes — assessed on depth, rate, and hand position.

lessons.title: Electricity and Circuits
lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.reading_material: Electric current (A) is the flow of charge. Voltage (V) drives the current. Resistance (Ω) opposes current flow. Ohm's Law: V = IR. In series circuits, current is the same throughout. In parallel circuits, voltage is the same across each branch.
practical_activities: Build and compare series and parallel circuits
Plot V-I graph to determine resistance
exercises: Calculate resistance if V=12V and I=3A
Compare brightness of bulbs in series vs parallel
lessons.homework: Investigate how resistance changes with the length of a wire.

revision.notes: V = IR — cover V to find IR, cover I to find V/R, cover R to find V/I.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: What is the formula for Ohm's Law?
In a parallel circuit, which quantity is the same in each branch?

lessons.assessment: Circuit analysis: Calculate missing values in 5 series and parallel circuit problems.

lessons.title: Magnetism and Electromagnetism
lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.reading_material: Magnets produce invisible force fields. An electric current in a wire produces a magnetic field. The motor effect: a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force. Electromagnetic induction: moving a conductor through a magnetic field generates an electric current (generator).
practical_activities: Map the field around a bar magnet using iron filings
Model the motor effect with a current-carrying wire (demonstration)
exercises: Apply Fleming's left-hand rule to find force direction
Explain how a transformer works
lessons.homework: Research how MRI machines use electromagnetism to image the human body.

revision.notes: Fleming's Left Hand = Motor (ForCe = thumb, Current = index, Field = middle finger).
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: Fleming's Left-Hand Rule is used for what?
What is electromagnetic induction?
options: Using current to make a magnet
Moving a conductor in a field to generate current
questions.correct: Moving a conductor in a field to generate current

lessons.assessment: Short answer: Explain how an electric motor works, including the motor effect.

lessons.title: Radioactivity and the Atom
lessons.subject: Physics
learning_objectives: Describe the structure of the nucleus
Distinguish alpha, beta, and gamma radiation
lessons.reading_material: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons. Unstable nuclei decay by emitting radiation. Alpha (α): helium nucleus — short range, stopped by paper. Beta (β): fast electron — stopped by aluminium. Gamma (γ): electromagnetic wave — stopped by lead.
practical_activities: Use a Geiger counter simulation to model decay
Plot a half-life graph
exercises: A sample has a half-life of 4 days. What fraction remains after 12 days?
Rank α, β, γ by penetrating power
lessons.homework: Calculate the remaining mass of a radioactive sample given half-life and time elapsed.

revision.notes: Half-life: after each half-life, exactly half of the remaining atoms have decayed.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: Which radiation has the GREATEST penetrating power?
What is half-life?
options: Time for all atoms to decay
Time for half the atoms to decay
questions.correct: Time for half the atoms to decay

lessons.assessment: Half-life calculation: Solve 3 half-life problems using a decay table.

lessons.title: Acids, Bases, and Salts
lessons.subject: Chemistry
lessons.reading_material: Acids release H⁺ ions in solution; bases accept H⁺ ions. pH measures acidity: 0-6 acid, 7 neutral, 8-14 alkaline. Acids and bases neutralise each other to form a salt and water.
practical_activities: Test household liquids with universal indicator
Prepare copper sulfate by neutralisation (supervised)
exercises: Write the equation for HCl + NaOH
Predict salt names from acid and base combinations
lessons.homework: Complete a table: acid + base → salt + water for 5 different combinations.

revision.notes: Acid + Base → Salt + Water — the general neutralisation equation.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: What is the pH of a neutral solution?
What is formed when an acid and base react?

lessons.assessment: Lab report: Describe the preparation of copper sulfate by neutralisation.

lessons.title: Moles and Stoichiometry
lessons.subject: Chemistry
learning_objectives: Calculate moles from mass and formula mass
Use mole ratios from balanced equations
lessons.reading_material: The mole is the SI unit for amount of substance (6.02 × 10²³ particles — Avogadro's number). Relative formula mass (Mr) is the sum of relative atomic masses. n = m ÷ Mr.
practical_activities: Calculate the Mr of common compounds
Solve mole calculation problems
exercises: Calculate moles in 40g of NaOH (Mr=40)
Find mass of CO₂ produced from 0.5 mol CaCO₃
lessons.homework: Solve a 5-step mole calculation problem from a given reaction.

revision.notes: n = m/Mr — learn this triangle: moles × Mr = mass, so mass ÷ Mr = moles.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: What is the Mr of H₂O?
How many moles in 56g of iron (Ar=56)?

lessons.assessment: Calculation: Find the mass of product formed from given amounts of reactants.

lessons.title: Organic Chemistry Basics
lessons.subject: Chemistry
lessons.reading_material: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds. Alkanes (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂) are saturated hydrocarbons; alkenes (CₙH₂ₙ) are unsaturated. Key reactions include combustion and addition reactions.
practical_activities: Model methane, ethane, ethene using ball-and-stick kits
Test alkene using bromine water (teacher demonstration)
exercises: Draw structural formulae for butane and but-1-ene
Write the equation for complete combustion of ethane
lessons.homework: Research petroleum fractions and explain the industrial importance of cracking.

revision.notes: Alkanes are SINGLE bonds only (saturated). Alkenes have at least one DOUBLE bond (unsaturated).
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: What is the general formula for alkanes?
Which reagent tests for the presence of a C=C double bond?

lessons.assessment: Name and draw the first four alkanes and write complete combustion equations.

lessons.title: Transport in Plants
lessons.subject: Biology
learning_objectives: Explain osmosis, diffusion, and active transport
Describe the role of xylem and phloem
lessons.reading_material: Plants transport water and minerals through xylem vessels and food (glucose) through phloem. Water moves up through transpiration — evaporation of water from leaves creates a pull that draws water up from roots.
practical_activities: Set up a potometer to measure transpiration rate
Compare transpiration in light vs dark conditions
exercises: Explain the transpiration stream step by step
Calculate water uptake from potometer data
lessons.homework: Design an investigation to test one factor affecting transpiration rate.

revision.notes: Xylem carries water UP (think: Xylophone keys go up); Phloem carries FOOD both ways.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: Which tissue carries water in plants?
What is transpiration?

lessons.assessment: Extended writing: Trace the journey of a water molecule from soil to leaf.

lessons.title: Genetics and Inheritance
lessons.subject: Biology
lessons.reading_material: Genes are sections of DNA that code for proteins. Alleles are different versions of a gene. Dominant alleles are expressed even when only one copy is present; recessive alleles only show when two copies are present.
practical_activities: Complete Punnett squares for monohybrid crosses
Predict offspring ratios
exercises: Calculate the probability of a tall plant from given parents
Construct a family pedigree chart
lessons.homework: Create a Punnett square for a cross between two parents heterozygous for dimples.

revision.notes: Use capital letters for dominant alleles (T) and lowercase for recessive (t). Tt = heterozygous = carrier.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: If T is dominant and t is recessive, what is the phenotype of Tt?
What ratio of phenotypes comes from a Tt × Tt cross?

lessons.assessment: Punnett square problem set: Solve 5 monohybrid cross problems.

lessons.title: Homeostasis
lessons.subject: Biology
learning_objectives: Describe blood glucose and temperature regulation
lessons.reading_material: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment. The body uses negative feedback: when conditions deviate from normal, a corrective response brings them back.
practical_activities: Model blood glucose regulation with a role-play activity
Analyse temperature regulation diagrams
exercises: Explain negative feedback using a thermostat analogy
Describe two effectors used in thermoregulation
lessons.homework: Create a flow diagram showing the regulation of blood glucose after a meal.

revision.notes: Think of homeostasis like a thermostat — it constantly detects and corrects to maintain a set point.
revision.tip: Review this lesson before the next class

questions.question: Which hormone lowers blood glucose?
What type of feedback mechanism does homeostasis use?

lessons.assessment: Essay: Explain how the body regulates blood glucose after eating a meal high in carbohydrates.

lessons.title: Ethics and Moral Philosophy
lessons.subject: Philosophy
learning_objectives: Apply utilitarianism to a moral dilemma
lessons.reading_material: Ethics asks: what makes actions right or wrong? Consequentialism (Utilitarianism) judges actions by their outcomes — the greatest good for the greatest number (Bentham, Mill). Deontology (Kant) says some actions are right or wrong regardless of consequences — follow universal duties. Virtue Ethics (Aristotle) focuses on the character of the agent rather than rules or outcomes. Each framework offers insight and faces objections.
practical_activities: The Trolley Problem discussion: apply all three frameworks and compare conclusions
exercises: Explain utilitarianism in your own words
Give one strength and one weakness of deontological ethics
What is the Categorical Imperative?
lessons.homework: Research Peter Singer's utilitarian argument on global poverty — do you agree? Write a short response.

revision.notes: Utilitarianism = best outcome for most. Deontology = follow duties. Virtue ethics = be a good person.
revision.tip: For any ethical dilemma, ask: consequences? duties? character?

quiz.question: Kant's Categorical Imperative asks you to
options: Act only on rules you could will to be universal laws
quiz.correct: Act only on rules you could will to be universal laws

lessons.assessment: Apply two ethical frameworks to the trolley problem and state which you find more convincing and why.

lessons.title: Evaluating Sources and Bias
lessons.subject: Critical Thinking
lessons.reading_material: Not all sources of information are equally reliable. Credibility depends on the author's expertise, the publication's reputation, the evidence cited, and whether the work is peer-reviewed. Bias is a tendency to favour one side. Confirmation bias means seeking only information that confirms existing beliefs. Media bias occurs when news outlets present events favourably for their political or commercial interests. Critical thinkers cross-check information across multiple reliable sources.
practical_activities: Fact-check a viral news headline using three different reliable sources
exercises: What criteria make a source credible?
Explain confirmation bias with a personal example
Why should you use multiple sources when researching?
lessons.homework: Choose a controversial topic, find two articles with opposing biases, and compare their arguments.

revision.notes: Credibility = expertise + evidence + peer review. Bias = one-sided perspective.

lessons.title: Human Resources and Motivation
lessons.subject: Business Studies
learning_objectives: Explain the role of human resources
lessons.reading_material: Human Resources (HR) manages the people in an organisation. Motivated employees work harder and are more productive. Frederick Taylor believed money was the main motivator (scientific management). Abraham Maslow proposed a hierarchy of needs — from basic (food, safety) to self-actualisation. Frederick Herzberg identified 'hygiene factors' (prevent dissatisfaction) and 'motivators' (drive satisfaction). Businesses use pay, promotion, recognition, and good working conditions to motivate staff.
practical_activities: Role-play: HR manager must motivate a team using only non-financial methods
exercises: Draw and label Maslow's hierarchy of needs
Give two financial and two non-financial methods of motivation
Explain one criticism of Taylor's scientific management
lessons.homework: Research a company known for employee satisfaction and identify what motivates their staff.

revision.notes: Taylor=money motivates; Maslow=hierarchy of needs; Herzberg=hygiene+motivators.
revision.tip: Use the acronym TMH (Taylor, Maslow, Herzberg) to remember the three theorists.

quiz.question: Which level is at the top of Maslow's hierarchy?

lessons.assessment: Case study: Describe how a manager could use TWO motivation theories to improve staff performance.
textbook_references: Cambridge IGCSE Business Studies — Hodder Education

lessons.title: International Relations
lessons.subject: World Politics
learning_objectives: Define key concepts: sovereignty, diplomacy, alliances
Describe the structure of the United Nations
Explain realism vs liberalism in international relations
lessons.reading_material: International Relations (IR) studies how countries, international organisations, and non-state actors interact. Sovereignty: a state's right to govern itself without external interference. Diplomacy: managing relations through negotiation. Realism: states act in self-interest, prioritising security and power (dominant during Cold War). Liberalism: cooperation through institutions (UN, WTO) can create mutual benefits. The UN has 6 principal organs: General Assembly, Security Council, Secretariat, ICJ, ECOSOC, Trusteeship Council.
practical_activities: Simulate a UN Security Council debate on a current global issue
exercises: Define sovereignty and explain why it is important
What is the difference between realism and liberalism in IR?
Name and explain 3 UN organs
lessons.homework: Research one international dispute being handled by the UN currently — what is its status?

revision.notes: Realism = power + self-interest. Liberalism = cooperation + institutions. UN has 6 organs.
revision.tip: Current events are the best textbook for IR — read international news daily.

quiz.correct: A country's right to self-govern without external interference
